prompt: How do the shop's metrics reach Prometheus?

choices.text: Each service sends them to Prometheus when a value changes
choices.why: That is push; Prometheus pulls.

choices.text: Prometheus asks each target for them on a schedule
choices.why: Right: a scrape, every fifteen seconds here.

choices.text: The Collector forwards them along with the traces
choices.why: In this lab the Collector carries traces and logs, not the shop's metrics.

choices.text: Loki extracts them from the log lines
choices.why: Loki stores logs.

prompt: A service that pushes its metrics crashes. What does the monitoring system notice?
hint: What does pull give Prometheus for free?

choices.text: Possibly nothing: the service just goes quiet
choices.why: Right. With pull, the failed scrape itself is recorded as `up` 0.

choices.text: An error, sent by the service as it crashes
choices.why: A crashing process rarely gets to send anything.

choices.text: The same as with pull: `up` becomes 0
choices.why: `up` exists because Prometheus does the asking.

choices.text: A gap that Prometheus fills with the last value it received from that service
choices.why: Nothing fills it in.

prompt: For every target, on every scrape, Prometheus records a metric called `___` that is 1 if the scrape worked and 0 if not.
Match each part of a line in the metrics text format to what it is.

pairs.right: The labels that make this one series

right_distractors: The time the request was made

prompt: Which selector returns every storefront series whose status code is a 4xx?

choices.text: `http_server_requests_total{job="storefront", code="4xx"}`
choices.why: `=` matches the literal text `4xx`, which no series has.

choices.text: `http_server_requests_total{job="storefront", code=~"4.."}`
choices.why: Right: `=~` takes a regular expression.

choices.text: `http_server_requests_total{job="storefront", code!="2.."}`
choices.why: `!=` is exact, and would not exclude 5xx either.

choices.text: `http_server_requests_total{job="storefront"} > 400`
choices.why: That compares the counter's value, not the code.

prompt: Why does `http_server_requests_total{code="201"}` = 281 tell you almost nothing on its own?

choices.text: 281 is below Prometheus's precision
choices.why: Precision is not the problem.

choices.text: Counters are reset by every scrape, so 281 covers fifteen seconds
choices.why: A scrape reads the counter; it resets nothing.

choices.text: It counts since the process started, whenever that was
choices.why: Right. Its rate is what carries information.

choices.text: The value is in thousands
choices.why: It is a plain count.

prompt: What does `rate(http_server_requests_total[1m])` answer?

choices.text: The number of requests in the last minute
choices.why: That is `increase()`.

choices.text: Requests per second, averaged over the last minute
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The fastest request of the last minute
choices.why: Counters say nothing about durations.

choices.text: How many times the counter was scraped in the last minute
choices.why: That would be four, whatever the traffic.

prompt: `rate(...[1m])` returned 4.222 for code 201 and 0.267 for 402. To two decimal places, how many checkouts per second is that in total?
The storefront restarted and its counter fell from 339 to 123. What did `rate()` over the restart do?

choices.text: It returned a negative rate for the minute of the restart
choices.why: That is what naive subtraction would give, and what `rate()` avoids.

choices.text: It returned nothing until the counter passed 339 again
choices.why: It kept answering throughout.

choices.text: Took the drop as a reset
choices.why: Right: it kept counting from zero, about five a second, as before.

choices.text: It averaged the old and new values
choices.why: No averaging of values happens.

prompt: To count how many times a counter went back to zero in a window, PromQL has the function `___()`.
`increase(...[1m])` returned 304.4 one day. How can a count of requests be fractional?

choices.text: Some requests are counted as half because they failed
choices.why: Every request counts as one.

choices.text: It extrapolates from the scrapes inside the window to the whole window
choices.why: Right. It is an estimate, not a tally.

choices.text: Prometheus stores counters as floats and rounding errors pile up
choices.why: The fraction is far larger than float rounding.

choices.text: The counter was reset in the middle of the window
choices.why: A reset is handled, and does not cause fractions.

prompt: Why alert on the share of failed charges instead of the rate of failures?
hint: Five requests a second or five thousand.

choices.text: Its meaning depends on traffic
choices.why: Right. The same rate of failures is alarming at five requests a second and nothing at five thousand; a share stays meaningful.

choices.text: Prometheus cannot alert on a rate
choices.why: It can alert on any expression.

choices.text: A share is cheaper to compute
choices.why: It costs more: two sums and a division.

choices.text: Rates are only available in recording rules
choices.why: `rate()` works anywhere.

prompt: Payments was told to fail every 20th charge, and the ratio came back as 0.0495. As a percentage, to the nearest whole number, how many charges fail?
Someone writes the ratio as errors over `[1m]` divided by total over `[5m]`. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: rates are per second, so windows do not matter
choices.why: Different windows average different periods.

choices.text: `[5m]` is not allowed in a division
choices.why: It is allowed; it is just wrong here.

choices.text: The two halves describe different periods, so the share is not a share of anything
choices.why: Right. Both sides need the same window.

choices.text: Errors must use `increase()` and totals `rate()`
choices.why: Mixing them would be wrong too.

prompt: Match each exporter to what it translates.
What can the blackbox exporter catch that the storefront's own metrics cannot?

choices.text: How many checkouts were declined
choices.why: The storefront counts those itself.

choices.text: Requests that never reach the storefront
choices.why: Right: a broken path in front of a healthy service.

choices.text: The storefront's memory use
choices.why: That is the machine's or the process's own metric.

choices.text: The trace id of a slow request
choices.why: A probe has no trace.

prompt: You add Redis to the shop. What is the first thing to look for?

choices.text: A way to make Redis push to the Pushgateway
choices.why: The Pushgateway is for jobs that end.

choices.text: An instrumentation package for OpenTelemetry traces
choices.why: That covers clients' calls, not Redis's own state.

choices.text: An existing Redis exporter
choices.why: Right. Almost everything already has one.

choices.text: A time to write a Redis exporter in Python from scratch
choices.why: Look before writing.

prompt: Why can Prometheus not scrape the nightly report directly?

choices.text: It has no HTTP server
choices.why: One could be added; the problem is time.

choices.text: It exits before the next scrape could arrive
choices.why: Right: about a second, against fifteen.

choices.text: Its metrics are traces
choices.why: It has a trace and metrics, separately.

choices.text: Jobs are not allowed in `scrape_configs`
choices.why: Any address can be a target.

prompt: Why does the report push a timestamp of its last success rather than a counter of runs?
hint: What happens on the night it does not run?

choices.text: Timestamps take less space in the Pushgateway
choices.why: Space is not the reason.

choices.text: Counters cannot be pushed
choices.why: They can.

choices.text: Its age grows when nothing runs
choices.why: Right: `time() -` it keeps growing, so an alert can fire on absence. A counter would just stay still.

choices.text: A timestamp also records which orders were counted
choices.why: It is one number.

prompt: Which of these are good reasons NOT to use the Pushgateway for a long-running service? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does it keep, and what does it lose?

choices.text: It keeps the last value after the service dies
choices.why: Yes: a dead service looks alive.

choices.text: The per-instance `up` from scraping is lost
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: It cannot store gauges
choices.why: The report pushed two.

choices.text: It requires TLS
choices.why: The lab's speaks plain HTTP.

prompt: What does a recording rule do?

choices.text: Records every query a dashboard sends
choices.why: It records the result of its own expression.

choices.text: Saves a result as a series
choices.why: Right: an expression's result, under a new name, computed once per evaluation.

choices.text: Sends an alert when a series is recorded
choices.why: That is an alerting rule.

choices.text: Saves the TSDB to disk
choices.why: Storage does that on its own.

prompt: Put the life of the PaymentsFailing alert in order.
hint: From the rule to the pager.
items: The ratio crosses 2% and the alert becomes pending
The condition holds for two minutes and the alert fires
Alertmanager groups it and sends it to the pager

prompt: The error ratio rises above 2% for 90 seconds and falls back. What happens with `for: 2m`?

choices.text: It fires for 90 seconds
choices.why: It never reaches firing.

choices.text: It goes pending, then back to inactive, and nobody is paged
choices.why: Right: a blip, not a page.

choices.text: It fires once the two minutes are up, even though the condition cleared
choices.why: The condition must hold throughout.

choices.text: Alertmanager receives it as resolved
choices.why: A pending alert is never sent.

prompt: Who decides that the PaymentsFailing page goes to the pager rather than to e-mail?
hint: Prometheus only decides that it fires.

choices.text: The rule's `severity: page` label, read by Prometheus
choices.why: The label is information; routing is not Prometheus's job.

choices.text: The pager, which subscribes to alerts it likes
choices.why: The pager only receives.

choices.text: Alertmanager's routes
choices.why: Right, and lesson 16 routes on that label.

choices.text: The Collector
choices.why: The Collector is not in the alert path.

prompt: The usual shape of an error ratio is `sum(rate(errors[1m])) / sum(___(all[1m]))`.
hint: The same function on both sides.
